verdicts.why: No finding claims that an attacker-controlled length field sizes an allocation made before the payload is proven to exist. The closest is F02 ('Underflow Risk: contentLength Comparison Uses Less-Than Instead of Less-Than-Equal', ValueReader.java:87), which does touch the same code and even quotes 'new byte[(int)contentLength]', but only in passing: what it says is exploitable is the boundary comparison ('if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)' admitting the exact value Integer.MAX_VALUE) and the resulting wrong exception type ('throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of a controlled MalformedFrameException'), and it even concedes 'Integer.MAX_VALUE as an int remains Integer.MAX_VALUE (no overflow in Java int cast)'. It never argues that a declared length lets an attacker force a large allocation without supplying the bytes. F05 is the only other memory-exhaustion finding, but its mechanism is an unvalidated BigDecimal scale, not a length-driven buffer allocation.

verdicts.quote: readFieldValue processes case 'F' (line 180-181) which calls readTable(), which calls readFieldValue() for each value. Similarly, case 'A' (line 183-184) calls readArray(), which calls readFieldValue(). No depth limit or recursion guard is present. Maximum nesting depth is unbounded.
verdicts.why: F07 is entirely about the mutual recursion cycle readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray -> readFieldValue with no depth counter, and states that the nesting in the attacker-supplied input controls the depth ('An attacker can send deeply nested structures ... to exhaust the stack via recursion, causing a StackOverflowError'). That is exactly D2's mechanism: decoding routines calling one another in a cycle with nothing counting the depth.
